histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are the three layers of the skin?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The epidermis (keratinised stratified squamous epithelium), the dermis (connective tissue), and the hypodermis (subcutaneous fat).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What type of epithelium forms the epidermis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are the functions of the skin?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Barrier/protection, thermoregulation, sensation, vitamin D synthesis, and immune defence.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: How does thick skin differ from thin skin?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Thick skin (palms/soles) has a very thick epidermis with a stratum lucidum and no hair follicles; thin skin (elsewhere) is thinner, has hair follicles and lacks a lucidum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: List the epidermal layers from deep to superficial.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin only), and corneum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What characterises the stratum basale?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: A single layer of dividing stem cells (keratinocytes) attached to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes; it also contains melanocytes and Merkel cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What characterises the stratum spinosum?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Several layers of 'prickle cells' joined by desmosomes; it contains Langerhans cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What characterises the stratum granulosum?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Cells containing basophilic keratohyalin granules and lipid-rich lamellar granules (waterproofing); the cells begin to die here.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Where is the stratum lucidum found?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Only in thick (palmoplantar) skin, as a clear layer just beneath the stratum corneum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is the stratum corneum?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The superficial layer of dead, flattened, anucleate keratin-filled corneocytes that forms the protective barrier.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is the epidermal turnover time?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Roughly 30–40 days from basal cell division to shedding at the surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are the four cell types of the epidermis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Keratinocytes, melanocytes, Langerhans cells, and Merkel cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is the origin and function of melanocytes?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Neural-crest-derived cells in the stratum basale that produce melanin and transfer it to keratinocytes via melanosomes for UV protection.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: How is melanin transferred and where is it stored?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Melanocytes package melanin into melanosomes and transfer it to surrounding keratinocytes, where it caps the nucleus to shield DNA from UV.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Do darker and lighter skin differ in melanocyte number?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: No — melanocyte numbers are similar; differences reflect the amount, type and distribution of melanin produced.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are Langerhans cells?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Bone-marrow-derived dendritic antigen-presenting cells in the stratum spinosum (containing Birbeck granules); part of skin immune surveillance.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are Merkel cells?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Mechanoreceptor cells in the stratum basale that mediate fine/sustained touch.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are the two layers of the dermis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The superficial papillary layer (loose CT with dermal papillae) and the deeper reticular layer (dense irregular CT).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is found in the papillary dermis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Loose connective tissue, dermal papillae that interdigitate with the epidermis, capillaries, and Meissner's corpuscles (light touch).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is found in the reticular dermis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Dense irregular connective tissue (collagen and elastic fibres), skin appendages, and Pacinian corpuscles (pressure/vibration).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is the hypodermis and its functions?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The subcutaneous layer of adipose and loose connective tissue providing insulation, energy storage and cushioning.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Which receptor detects light touch and where is it?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Meissner's corpuscle, in the dermal papillae (papillary dermis).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Which receptor detects deep pressure and vibration and where is it?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The Pacinian corpuscle, in the deep (reticular) dermis/hypodermis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Which receptor detects skin stretch?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Ruffini endings.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Which endings detect pain and temperature?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Free nerve endings.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is basal cell carcinoma and its behaviour?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The commonest skin cancer, arising from basal keratinocytes; it has a pearly rolled edge and rarely metastasises.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What histological feature characterises squamous cell carcinoma?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Keratin pearls (concentric whorls of keratinising cells); it is UV-related and can metastasise.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: From which cell does melanoma arise and how is prognosis assessed?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: From melanocytes; prognosis is assessed mainly by Breslow thickness (depth of invasion).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are the histological features of psoriasis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Parakeratosis (retained nuclei in the corneum), acanthosis (thickened spinosum), elongated rete ridges, and neutrophilic Munro microabscesses.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is spongiosis and which condition shows it?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Intercellular oedema of the epidermis; characteristic of eczema/dermatitis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Contrast pemphigus and pemphigoid.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Pemphigus (vulgaris) is intra-epidermal blistering from anti-desmoglein (desmosome) antibodies; bullous pemphigoid is subepidermal blistering from anti-hemidesmosome antibodies.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What causes vitiligo versus albinism?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Vitiligo is autoimmune destruction of melanocytes (patchy depigmentation); albinism is a genetic defect in melanin synthesis (melanocytes present but non-functional).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the pilosebaceous unit?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: The functional unit of the hair follicle, its sebaceous gland, and the arrector pili muscle (with an apocrine gland in some regions).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: From what do hair follicles and sebaceous glands develop?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: They are epidermal derivatives — down-growths of the epidermis into the dermis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What are the functions of sebum?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: To lubricate and waterproof the hair and skin, with mild antibacterial action.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Which skin lacks hair follicles?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Glabrous (hairless) skin — the palms and soles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What are the three regions of a hair follicle from surface to base?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: The infundibulum (surface to sebaceous duct), the isthmus, and the bulb at the base.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What does the hair bulb contain?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: The dermal papilla (vascular connective tissue that induces hair growth) surrounded by the proliferating matrix (with melanocytes).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the role of the dermal papilla?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: It is the inductive, vascular connective-tissue core that signals the matrix to grow hair.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the hair matrix and what does it do?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: The zone of proliferating cells around the dermal papilla that produces the hair shaft; it also contains melanocytes that colour the hair.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What are the three concentric layers of the hair shaft from inside out?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Medulla → cortex (keratin and pigment) → cuticle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What sheaths surround the hair within the follicle?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: The inner root sheath, the outer root sheath (continuous with the epidermis), a glassy (basement) membrane, and a connective-tissue sheath.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Why does hair grey with age?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Because the melanocytes in the hair matrix decline, so less pigment is added to the growing hair.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Name the three phases of the hair growth cycle.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Anagen (active growth, lasting years), catagen (brief regression), and telogen (rest, followed by shedding).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Where are hair follicle stem cells located?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: In the 'bulge' region at the isthmus, near the insertion of the arrector pili muscle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is telogen effluvium?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Diffuse hair shedding when a physiological stress (illness, childbirth, surgery) pushes many follicles synchronously into the telogen (resting/shedding) phase; usually reversible.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What type of secretion do sebaceous glands use?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Holocrine secretion — the whole cell fills with lipid and disintegrates to release sebum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Where do most sebaceous glands empty?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Into the hair follicle (via the pilosebaceous canal).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What stimulates sebaceous gland activity?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Androgens — which is why the glands enlarge and sebum increases at puberty.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the arrector pili muscle and its innervation?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: A slip of smooth muscle from the follicle bulge to the papillary dermis, under sympathetic control.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What does contraction of the arrector pili produce?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Hair erection ('goosebumps') and expression of sebum from the sebaceous gland.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Give examples of sebaceous glands that open directly onto the surface (not into hair).
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Meibomian (tarsal) glands of the eyelid, Montgomery glands of the areola, and glands of the lips.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the pathophysiology of acne vulgaris?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Follicular hyperkeratinisation and excess (androgen-driven) sebum, with Cutibacterium acnes colonisation and inflammation, producing comedones, papules and pustules.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What organism is implicated in acne?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is androgenetic alopecia and how is it treated?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Progressive follicle miniaturisation driven by dihydrotestosterone (DHT); treated with minoxidil and finasteride.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is alopecia areata?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Autoimmune, non-scarring patchy hair loss, classically with 'exclamation-mark' hairs at the edges.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is a 'sebaceous cyst'?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: A keratin-filled cyst arising from the follicle; most so-called sebaceous cysts are actually epidermoid or pilar (trichilemmal) cysts.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is hirsutism and a common cause?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Androgen-driven growth of terminal hair in a male pattern in women; commonly due to polycystic ovary syndrome.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is folliculitis / a furuncle?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Inflammation/infection of a hair follicle (folliculitis) or a deeper follicular abscess (furuncle/boil), often caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is a chalazion?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: A blocked/inflamed Meibomian (tarsal) gland of the eyelid, forming a painless lid lump (a stye involves the gland of Zeis and is usually acute/tender).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: How do the three modes of glandular secretion differ (with skin examples)?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Merocrine = exocytosis (eccrine sweat); apocrine = apical cytoplasm lost (apocrine sweat); holocrine = whole cell lost (sebaceous gland).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What signals sebaceous tumours may indicate systemically?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Multiple sebaceous neoplasms can be a marker of Muir–Torre syndrome (a variant of Lynch syndrome).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the difference between vellus and terminal hair?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Vellus hair is fine, short and unpigmented; terminal hair is coarse, long and pigmented (e.g. scalp, beard).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Why does the outer root sheath being continuous with the epidermis matter?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: It provides a reservoir of keratinocyte stem cells that can re-epithelialise the skin after superficial wounds/burns.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What are the two types of sweat gland?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Eccrine (merocrine) sweat glands and apocrine sweat glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is the basic structure of a sweat gland?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: A coiled tubular gland in the dermis, comprising a secretory coil and a duct.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Where are eccrine sweat glands found?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Throughout the skin (most dense on the palms, soles and forehead).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Where do eccrine sweat glands open?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Directly onto the skin surface via a sweat pore.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is the main function of eccrine sweat glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Thermoregulation by evaporative cooling.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What cell types make up the eccrine secretory coil?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Clear cells (secreting watery fluid of water and electrolytes), dark cells (secreting glycoprotein), and peripheral myoepithelial cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is the role of the myoepithelial cells in sweat glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: They contract to expel the secretion from the secretory coil into the duct.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What does the eccrine duct do to the sweat and why?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: It reabsorbs Na+ and Cl-, making the final sweat hypotonic (conserving salt).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: By what mechanism do eccrine glands secrete?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Merocrine secretion (exocytosis), with no loss of cytoplasm.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is unusual about the autonomic control of eccrine glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: They are controlled by sympathetic cholinergic (acetylcholine) nerves, unlike most sympathetic targets which are adrenergic.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Where are apocrine sweat glands located?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: In the axilla, areola, genital/perianal region, external ear (ceruminous) and eyelid (Moll's glands).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: When do apocrine glands become active?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: At puberty, under androgen influence.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Where do apocrine sweat glands empty?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Into the hair follicle (not directly onto the surface).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is the nature of apocrine secretion?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: A viscous, protein- and lipid-rich fluid that is odourless until broken down by skin bacteria.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Why does apocrine sweat cause body odour?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Skin bacteria metabolise its protein/lipid components, producing odorous compounds (bromhidrosis).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What autonomic nerves control apocrine glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Sympathetic adrenergic nerves.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Which modified apocrine glands produce earwax?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Ceruminous glands of the external auditory canal.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What are Moll's glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Modified apocrine glands of the eyelid margin.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: How does the sweat test diagnose cystic fibrosis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: In CF the defective CFTR channel prevents chloride (and sodium) reabsorption in the sweat duct, so sweat chloride is abnormally high.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Why is sweat normally hypotonic?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: The duct reabsorbs NaCl from the isotonic primary secretion faster than water, leaving a dilute (hypotonic) final sweat.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is hyperhidrosis and how can it be treated?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Excessive eccrine sweating; treated with topical antiperspirants (aluminium salts) or botulinum toxin, which blocks acetylcholine release.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Why does botulinum toxin reduce eccrine sweating?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: It blocks acetylcholine release at the cholinergic sympathetic nerve endings that stimulate eccrine glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is hidradenitis suppurativa?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: A chronic inflammatory disease of apocrine-gland-bearing skin (axillae, groin) with occlusion, painful nodules, sinus tracts and scarring.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is miliaria?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: 'Heat rash' caused by blockage of eccrine sweat ducts, trapping sweat and producing an itchy vesicular rash.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is anhidrosis and a genetic cause?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Absent/reduced sweating causing heat intolerance; a cause is ectodermal dysplasia (with reduced/absent sweat glands).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Distinguish the openings of eccrine and apocrine glands.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Eccrine glands open onto the skin surface; apocrine glands open into the hair follicle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Compare the innervation of eccrine and apocrine glands.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Eccrine glands are sympathetic cholinergic; apocrine glands are sympathetic adrenergic.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Which gland type is responsible for thermoregulatory sweating?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Eccrine sweat glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: How does the eccrine duct wall appear histologically?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: As a two-layered (stratified cuboidal) darker, more eosinophilic tubule, smaller than the secretory coil.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is bromhidrosis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Malodorous body odour from bacterial breakdown of apocrine secretions.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is Fox–Fordyce disease?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: A chronic condition of apocrine duct obstruction causing itchy follicular papules in apocrine-bearing skin.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Why are eccrine glands important in a hot environment or fever?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Their evaporative sweat is the body's main mechanism for dissipating heat and lowering core temperature.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What are the three tunics (coats) of the eye?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: The fibrous coat (sclera + cornea), the vascular coat/uvea (choroid, ciliary body, iris), and the neural coat (retina).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Which three structures perform the eye's optical work?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: The cornea (main refraction), the lens (accommodation/fine focus), and the retina (phototransduction).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: List the five layers of the cornea from anterior to posterior.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Epithelium, Bowman's layer, stroma (substantia propria), Descemet's membrane, and endothelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What type of epithelium covers the cornea and how does it regenerate?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, regenerated from limbal stem cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What makes up ~90% of the corneal thickness and gives transparency?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: The stroma — regularly arranged collagen lamellae with keratocytes; the regular spacing provides transparency.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is the function of the corneal endothelium?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: A single cell layer that pumps water out of the stroma to keep the cornea dehydrated and clear; it does not regenerate.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Why is loss of corneal endothelial cells (e.g. Fuchs' dystrophy) important?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: The endothelial pump fails, the stroma becomes oedematous, and the cornea clouds; the cells cannot be replaced.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: How is the avascular cornea nourished and oxygenated?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: By the tear film (oxygen from air), the aqueous humour, and the limbal blood vessels at its edge.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Why is the retina described as 'inverted'?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Light must pass through the inner retinal layers to reach the photoreceptors located at the back (outer) part.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is the signal pathway through the retina?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Photoreceptor (rod/cone) → bipolar cell → ganglion cell → optic nerve.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Contrast rods and cones.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Rods mediate dim/night vision (rhodopsin) and are peripheral; cones mediate colour and high-acuity vision and are concentrated at the fovea.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What are the functions of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: It phagocytoses shed photoreceptor discs, stores/regenerates vitamin A (retinal), absorbs stray light, and forms the outer blood-retinal barrier.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is special about the fovea?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: It contains only cones, provides the highest visual acuity, and is an avascular pit (photoreceptors displaced aside so light reaches them directly).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is the optic disc and why is it the blind spot?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: The point where ganglion-cell axons exit as the optic nerve and vessels enter; it has no photoreceptors, so it is the blind spot.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What are Müller cells?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: The principal glial (supporting) cells of the retina, spanning its full thickness.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Describe the structure of the lens.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: An avascular biconvex structure with a thick capsule (basement membrane), an anterior epithelium, and elongated lens fibres packed with crystallins that have lost their organelles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What suspends the lens and from where?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Zonular fibres (suspensory ligament) attaching it to the ciliary body.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Explain accommodation for near vision.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: The ciliary muscle contracts, which relaxes the zonular fibres, allowing the elastic lens to become more rounded (increasing its refractive power).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Why are lens fibres transparent?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: They lose their nuclei and organelles and are packed with regularly arranged crystallin proteins.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What does the ciliary body do?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: It contains the ciliary muscle (accommodation) and the ciliary processes that secrete aqueous humour.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What controls pupil size?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: The sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic, constricts the pupil) and the dilator pupillae (sympathetic, dilates the pupil) in the iris.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Trace the flow of aqueous humour.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Produced by the ciliary body → posterior chamber → through the pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork → canal of Schlemm → venous drainage.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What causes glaucoma?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Impaired aqueous drainage raising intraocular pressure, which damages the optic nerve and causes optic disc cupping.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is a cataract?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Opacification of the lens (aggregation of crystallin proteins) causing painless, progressive visual loss; risk factors include ageing, diabetes and steroids.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is age-related macular degeneration?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Damage to the RPE and photoreceptors at the macula (with drusen deposits) causing loss of central vision.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What are the retinal changes in diabetic retinopathy?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Microaneurysms, dot-and-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots and, in proliferative disease, neovascularisation.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is a retinal detachment?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Separation of the neural retina from the retinal pigment epithelium, causing sudden painless visual field loss (a 'curtain').

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is retinitis pigmentosa?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: A progressive inherited degeneration of rods causing night blindness and peripheral (tunnel) vision loss, with pigment deposition in the retina.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is the sclera?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: The tough white dense connective-tissue outer coat that maintains the shape of the eye and gives attachment to the extraocular muscles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What does the choroid do?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: A vascular, pigmented layer between retina and sclera that supplies blood to the outer retina and absorbs stray light.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: What is the histological hallmark of retinoblastoma?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes; it is a childhood retinal tumour linked to mutation of the RB1 tumour-suppressor gene.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.front: Why does vitamin A deficiency cause night blindness?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.back: Vitamin A (retinal) is required to form rhodopsin in rods; its deficiency impairs rod function and dim-light vision.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What are the three parts of the ear?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: The external ear (pinna, canal, tympanic membrane), the middle ear (ossicles), and the inner ear (cochlea and vestibular apparatus).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What two senses does the inner ear serve?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Hearing (cochlea/organ of Corti) and balance (vestibular apparatus).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is the pinna made of?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Elastic cartilage covered by skin.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What glands are found in the external auditory canal?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Ceruminous glands (modified apocrine glands producing earwax) and sebaceous glands, with hairs.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What are the three layers of the tympanic membrane?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: An outer stratified squamous epithelium, a middle fibrous layer, and an inner cuboidal (mucosal) layer.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: Name the three middle-ear ossicles in order.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Malleus, incus, and stapes.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is the function of the ossicles?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: To amplify and transmit sound vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the oval window, overcoming the impedance of the inner-ear fluid.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is the role of the Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: It connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalises middle-ear pressure with atmospheric pressure.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: Which ossicle contacts the oval window?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: The stapes (its footplate sits in the oval window).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: Name the three chambers of the cochlea and their fluids.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Scala vestibuli (perilymph), scala media/cochlear duct (endolymph), and scala tympani (perilymph).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: Where does the organ of Corti sit?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: On the basilar membrane within the scala media (cochlear duct).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: Contrast inner and outer hair cells.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Inner hair cells are the main sensory cells providing afferent signals to the cochlear nerve; outer hair cells amplify basilar-membrane vibrations.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: How is sound transduced in the organ of Corti?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Sound vibrates the basilar membrane, bending the hair-cell stereocilia against the overlying tectorial membrane, depolarising the hair cells and generating signals in the cochlear nerve (CN VIII).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is the tectorial membrane?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: The gelatinous membrane overlying the organ of Corti against which the hair-cell stereocilia bend during sound stimulation.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is tonotopy in the cochlea?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: The spatial mapping of frequency: the stiff narrow base detects high frequencies and the wide floppy apex detects low frequencies.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: How do endolymph and perilymph differ?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Endolymph is high in potassium (in the scala media, produced by the stria vascularis); perilymph is high in sodium (in the scala vestibuli and tympani).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What produces endolymph?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: The stria vascularis in the wall of the cochlear duct.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: Which cranial nerve carries auditory signals?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: The cochlear division of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What are the sensory organs of the vestibular apparatus?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: The maculae of the utricle and saccule, and the cristae ampullares of the three semicircular canals.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What do the maculae detect and how?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Linear acceleration and gravity, via hair cells whose stereocilia are embedded in an otolithic membrane weighted with otoliths (calcium carbonate crystals).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What do the cristae ampullares detect and how?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Angular (rotational) acceleration, via hair cells projecting into a gelatinous cupula in the ampulla of each semicircular canal.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is distinctive about vestibular hair cell stereocilia?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: They have a bundle of stereocilia plus a single kinocilium; bending toward the kinocilium depolarises the cell.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is conductive hearing loss and its causes?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Impaired sound transmission through the external/middle ear — e.g. wax impaction, otitis media, or otosclerosis (stapes fixation).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is otosclerosis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Abnormal bone remodelling fixing the stapes footplate at the oval window, causing conductive hearing loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is sensorineural hearing loss and its causes?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Loss due to cochlear or CN VIII pathology — e.g. presbycusis, noise damage, ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, cisplatin) or acoustic neuroma.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: Why does presbycusis/noise damage cause high-frequency loss first?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: The outer hair cells at the cochlear base (which encode high frequencies) are the most vulnerable and are lost first.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is Ménière's disease?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph) causing episodic vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What causes benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: Displaced otoliths (otoconia) entering a semicircular canal, causing brief vertigo on head position change.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is a cholesteatoma?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: A collection of keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear that can erode bone and cause complications.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What is an acoustic neuroma?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: A vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle causing unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: What do Rinne and Weber tests distinguish?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: They differentiate conductive from sensorineural hearing loss using tuning-fork comparisons of air/bone conduction and lateralisation.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.front: Why must the ossicles amplify sound?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.back: To overcome the impedance mismatch between air in the middle ear and fluid in the inner ear, so vibrations are efficiently transmitted.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What is the function of the olfactory epithelium and where is it located?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: It detects odorants (the sense of smell) and lies in the roof of the nasal cavity (superior concha and adjacent septum).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What type of epithelium is the olfactory epithelium?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: A specialised (tall) pseudostratified columnar epithelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Which features distinguish olfactory from respiratory epithelium?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: The olfactory epithelium is taller, has no goblet cells, bears non-motile olfactory cilia, and has Bowman's glands and olfactory nerve bundles in the lamina propria.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Which cranial nerve carries olfactory signals?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Cranial nerve I (the olfactory nerve).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Name the three cell types of the olfactory epithelium.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Olfactory receptor neurons, sustentacular (supporting) cells, and basal cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Describe the olfactory receptor neurons.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Bipolar neurons whose dendrite ends in an olfactory knob bearing non-motile cilia (with odorant receptors); their axons form CN I. They are the only neurons directly exposed to the environment.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What are the olfactory cilia and are they motile?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Non-motile cilia projecting from the olfactory knob that carry the odorant receptors; unlike respiratory cilia they do not beat.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What do sustentacular (supporting) cells do?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: They are tall columnar cells with apical microvilli that support, insulate and metabolically assist the receptor neurons.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What is the role of basal cells in the olfactory epithelium?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: They are stem cells that regenerate the receptor neurons and sustentacular cells throughout life.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What are Bowman's glands and their function?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Serous glands in the lamina propria whose secretion dissolves odorants and keeps the epithelial surface moist.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Why must odorants dissolve before detection?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Odorant receptors on the cilia respond only to dissolved molecules, so odorants must first dissolve in the mucus/serous fluid from Bowman's glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Outline the signal-transduction cascade for smell.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: An odorant binds a receptor on the cilia → activates a G-protein (Golf) → raises cAMP → opens ion channels → the neuron depolarises and fires an action potential.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Where do olfactory axons go after leaving the epithelium?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: They pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to synapse in the olfactory bulb (in glomeruli with mitral cells), then via the olfactory tract to the cortex.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Why is olfaction unique among the senses in its central pathway?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: It is the only sensory system that reaches the cerebral cortex without first relaying in the thalamus.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What is remarkable about olfactory receptor neurons compared with other neurons?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: They are continuously replaced (regenerated from basal cells) throughout life — one of the few sites of adult neurogenesis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What bone do olfactory nerve axons pass through?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What are mitral cells?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: The output neurons of the olfactory bulb that receive input in glomeruli and project via the olfactory tract.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What are common causes of anosmia?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Head trauma (shearing of olfactory nerves at the cribriform plate), viral infection (URTI/COVID-19), nasal obstruction (polyps/congestion), ageing, and neurodegeneration.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: How can head trauma cause anosmia?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: A blow can shear the delicate olfactory nerve filaments where they cross the cribriform plate, disconnecting the epithelium from the bulb.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: How does COVID-19 cause loss of smell?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: SARS-CoV-2 infects the sustentacular (supporting) cells of the olfactory epithelium, disrupting olfactory function (usually reversible).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Which neurodegenerative diseases feature early anosmia?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease often have anosmia as an early feature.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What is Kallmann syndrome?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Anosmia combined with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, due to failed embryological migration of GnRH-secreting and olfactory neurons.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What is esthesioneuroblastoma?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: An olfactory neuroblastoma — a malignant tumour arising from the olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Why can a cribriform-plate fracture cause CSF rhinorrhoea?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: The fracture breaches the barrier between the cranial cavity and the nasal roof, allowing cerebrospinal fluid to leak into the nose (with a meningitis risk).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What colour does olfactory epithelium often appear grossly and why?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Yellowish-brown, due to lipofuscin pigment in the sustentacular cells and Bowman's glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Why does olfactory ability decline with age?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Progressive loss of receptor neurons and reduced regenerative capacity of basal cells reduce the number of functioning receptors.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What type of secretion do Bowman's glands produce?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: A watery serous secretion.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Which cell type is the primary sensory transducer of smell?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: The olfactory receptor neuron (via its ciliary odorant receptors).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: How do olfactory receptor neurons differ from most CNS neurons regarding replacement?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Unlike most neurons, they are continuously replaced from basal stem cells throughout adult life.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What is the pathway of an olfactory signal from cilium to cortex?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Cilium receptor → receptor-neuron axon → cribriform plate → olfactory bulb (glomerulus/mitral cell) → olfactory tract → olfactory cortex (bypassing the thalamus).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: Why is loss of smell clinically useful as an early sign?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Because it can precede other features — e.g. in COVID-19 and before the motor signs of Parkinson's disease.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.front: What separates the olfactory epithelium's neurons from the rest of the nervous system in terms of exposure?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.back: Their receptive dendrites/cilia are directly exposed to the external (nasal) environment, unlike protected CNS neurons.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What are taste buds and where are they found?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Barrel-shaped clusters of chemoreceptor cells in the stratified squamous epithelium of the tongue papillae (and soft palate, epiglottis, pharynx) that detect taste.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What are the five basic tastes?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Through what structure do tastants reach the taste-bud cells?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: The taste pore, into which microvilli ('gustatory hairs') project.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: On which papillae are taste buds found, and on which are they absent?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Present on fungiform, circumvallate and foliate papillae; absent on filiform papillae.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Describe filiform papillae.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: The most numerous papillae — keratinised and pointed, providing a rough gripping surface; they have NO taste buds.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Describe fungiform papillae.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Mushroom-shaped papillae on the anterior tongue, each with a few taste buds on its upper surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Describe circumvallate (vallate) papillae.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Large papillae (~8–12) arranged in a V at the back of the tongue, each surrounded by a moat/trench, bearing many taste buds and flushed by von Ebner's glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What are von Ebner's glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Serous glands that empty into the trenches of the circumvallate papillae, flushing away tastants so new ones can be sensed (and secreting lingual lipase).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Describe foliate papillae.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Leaf-like folds on the lateral tongue that carry taste buds, prominent in children but regressing in adults.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What is the general shape and span of a taste bud?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: An ovoid, barrel-shaped cluster of ~50–100 cells spanning the full epithelial thickness, opening at an apical taste pore.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What does the type I taste cell do?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: It is the most numerous, glial-like supporting cell, also implicated in salt sensing and housekeeping.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What does the type II taste cell detect and how?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Sweet, bitter and umami tastants, via G-protein-coupled receptors (T1R/T2R); it releases ATP rather than using a classic synapse.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What does the type III taste cell detect and how does it signal?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Sour taste; it forms a true synapse with the gustatory sensory nerve.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What is the role of basal cells in the taste bud?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: They are stem cells that continuously regenerate the taste cells (turnover ~10–14 days).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Are taste receptor cells neurons?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: No — they are specialised epithelial cells that synapse with (or signal to) sensory nerve fibres; they are continually replaced.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: How are salty and sour tastes transduced?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Salty via sodium (Na+) ion channels and sour via hydrogen ions (H+); sweet, bitter and umami use GPCRs.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Which nerve carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: The facial nerve (CN VII), via the chorda tympani.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Which nerve carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Which nerve carries taste from the epiglottis and pharynx?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: The vagus nerve (CN X).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Where do all taste afferents first synapse centrally?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: In the nucleus of the solitary tract (nucleus solitarius) in the medulla, then relay to the thalamus and gustatory cortex.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Why must tastants dissolve before being sensed?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Taste receptors on the microvilli respond only to dissolved molecules, so tastants must first dissolve in saliva.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What is the difference between taste and flavour?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Taste is the five basic modalities detected by taste buds; flavour is the combined perception of taste plus smell (and texture/temperature).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Why does a blocked nose or anosmia reduce 'taste'?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Much of perceived flavour comes from smell; without olfaction, food seems bland even though basic tastes are intact.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What are common causes of ageusia/dysgeusia?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Drugs, zinc deficiency, chemotherapy/radiotherapy, viral infection (e.g. COVID-19), and nerve lesions.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: How can a facial nerve (VII) lesion affect taste?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: It can damage the chorda tympani, causing loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (e.g. in Bell's palsy).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What is geographic tongue?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: A benign migratory loss of filiform papillae producing map-like red patches with pale borders on the tongue.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Why do many taste disturbances recover over time?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Because taste cells regenerate from basal stem cells, so post-viral or post-radiotherapy taste loss often partially recovers.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Why is taste often blunted in the elderly?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Taste-bud numbers and regenerative capacity decline with age, reducing taste sensitivity.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: How does radiotherapy to the head/neck affect taste?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: It damages taste cells and reduces salivary flow, causing taste disturbance that often partly recovers afterwards.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: Which tastant type historically was thought to be sensed only at the tongue tip (now known to be a myth)?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Sweet — the 'tongue map' of regional taste zones is a myth; all taste qualities are detectable across the tongue.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What is umami and its typical trigger?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: The savoury taste, triggered by glutamate (e.g. monosodium glutamate), sensed by type II cells via GPCRs.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.front: What secretes lingual lipase in the mouth?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.back: Von Ebner's glands (serous glands of the circumvallate papilla trenches).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The epidermis is composed of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The epidermis is keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The correct order of epidermal layers from deep to superficial is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Deep to superficial: basale → spinosum → granulosum → lucidum → corneum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The stratum lucidum is found only in:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The stratum lucidum is present only in thick skin of the palms and soles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Cell division in the epidermis occurs mainly in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The stratum basale contains the dividing stem cells that renew the epidermis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: 'Prickle cells' joined by desmosomes are found in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The stratum spinosum consists of prickle cells connected by desmosomes.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Melanocytes are located in the ______ and are derived from ______.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Melanocytes lie in the stratum basale and are neural-crest-derived; they transfer melanin to keratinocytes.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Melanin protects the skin by:
options: Shielding keratinocyte DNA from UV radiation
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Melanin caps keratinocyte nuclei, absorbing UV and protecting DNA from damage.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Langerhans cells are:
options: Dendritic antigen-presenting cells in the spinosum
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Langerhans cells are bone-marrow-derived dendritic antigen-presenting cells in the stratum spinosum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Merkel cells function as:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Merkel cells in the basal layer are mechanoreceptors for fine/sustained touch.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Which receptor detects light touch and lies in the dermal papillae?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Meissner's corpuscles in the papillary dermis detect light touch.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Which receptor detects deep pressure and vibration?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles in the deep dermis detect pressure and vibration.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The waterproofing lipid of the epidermis is released from:
options: Lamellar granules in the stratum granulosum
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Lamellar (membrane-coating) granules in the stratum granulosum release lipid that waterproofs the epidermis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The two layers of the dermis are the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The dermis has a superficial papillary layer and a deeper reticular layer.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The hypodermis consists mainly of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The hypodermis (subcutis) is mainly adipose tissue providing insulation and cushioning.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The commonest skin cancer, arising from basal keratinocytes, is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the commonest skin cancer; it has a pearly rolled edge and rarely metastasises.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Keratin pearls are a histological feature of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Keratin pearls (concentric keratinising whorls) are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The prognosis of melanoma is best assessed by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Breslow thickness (depth of tumour invasion) is the key prognostic factor in melanoma.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Psoriasis characteristically shows:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Psoriasis shows parakeratosis, acanthosis, elongated rete ridges and neutrophilic Munro microabscesses.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Pemphigus vulgaris causes blistering by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is intra-epidermal blistering from anti-desmoglein (desmosome) antibodies; pemphigoid is subepidermal (hemidesmosome).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Spongiosis (intercellular epidermal oedema) is typical of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Spongiosis — intercellular oedema of the epidermis — is characteristic of eczema/dermatitis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The pilosebaceous unit consists of:
options: Hair follicle + sebaceous gland + arrector pili muscle
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The pilosebaceous unit is the hair follicle, its sebaceous gland and the arrector pili muscle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The inductive, vascular core at the base of the hair bulb is the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The dermal papilla is the vascular connective-tissue core that induces hair growth; the matrix around it proliferates.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The cells that produce the hair shaft are in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The matrix (around the dermal papilla) is the proliferating zone that produces the hair shaft.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The layers of the hair shaft from inside out are:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: From inside out the hair shaft is medulla → cortex → cuticle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Hair colour is determined by melanocytes located in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Melanocytes in the matrix add pigment to the growing hair; their decline causes greying.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The active growth phase of the hair cycle is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Anagen is the active growth phase (lasting years); catagen is regression and telogen is rest/shedding.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Hair follicle stem cells reside in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Follicular stem cells lie in the bulge at the isthmus, near the arrector pili insertion.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Sebaceous glands secrete by which mechanism?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Sebaceous glands are holocrine — the entire lipid-laden cell disintegrates to release sebum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Sebaceous glands normally empty into the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Most sebaceous glands empty into the hair follicle via the pilosebaceous canal.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Sebaceous gland activity is stimulated by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Androgens stimulate sebaceous glands, which is why sebum production increases at puberty.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The arrector pili muscle is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The arrector pili is smooth muscle innervated by the sympathetic system; it raises the hair and expresses sebum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Which skin lacks hair follicles and sebaceous glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Glabrous skin of the palms and soles has no hair follicles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Acne vulgaris involves all of the following EXCEPT:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Acne results from follicular plugging, excess sebum, C. acnes and inflammation — not melanocyte destruction.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Androgenetic alopecia is caused by follicle miniaturisation driven by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: DHT drives progressive follicle miniaturisation in androgenetic alopecia; finasteride blocks its formation.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Diffuse hair shedding after childbirth or severe illness is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: A stressor synchronises many follicles into telogen, causing reversible diffuse shedding (telogen effluvium).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: A blocked Meibomian gland of the eyelid produces a:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: A chalazion is a blocked/inflamed Meibomian (tarsal) sebaceous gland of the eyelid.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Which is an example of a sebaceous gland opening directly onto the surface?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Meibomian glands (and Montgomery glands of the areola) are sebaceous glands opening directly onto the surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The 'holocrine' mode of secretion means:
options: The whole cell disintegrates to release its product
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: In holocrine secretion the entire cell breaks down to form the secretion (as in sebaceous glands).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Alopecia areata is best described as:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Alopecia areata is autoimmune, non-scarring patchy hair loss with exclamation-mark hairs.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Multiple sebaceous neoplasms can be a marker of which syndrome?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Sebaceous tumours can indicate Muir–Torre syndrome, a variant of Lynch syndrome (mismatch-repair defect).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Eccrine sweat glands open:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands open directly onto the skin surface via a pore; apocrine glands open into hair follicles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The main function of eccrine sweat glands is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands produce watery sweat for evaporative cooling (thermoregulation).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which cells of the eccrine secretory coil produce the watery component of sweat?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Clear cells secrete the watery fluid (water and electrolytes); dark cells secrete glycoprotein.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The eccrine sweat duct modifies the primary secretion by:
options: Reabsorbing Na+ and Cl- to make sweat hypotonic
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: The duct reabsorbs NaCl faster than water, producing hypotonic sweat.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Eccrine sweat glands are controlled by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Uniquely, eccrine glands are innervated by sympathetic cholinergic (ACh) fibres.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Apocrine sweat glands are found in the:
options: Axilla, groin, areola and external ear
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands are restricted to the axilla, groin, areola, external ear and eyelid.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Apocrine sweat glands open into the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands empty into the hair follicle, not directly onto the surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Apocrine glands become functionally active:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands develop and become active at puberty under androgen influence.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Body odour from apocrine sweat is due to:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine secretion is odourless until skin bacteria metabolise it, producing body odour.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Ceruminous glands (which produce earwax) are modified:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Ceruminous glands of the ear canal are modified apocrine glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: In cystic fibrosis, sweat chloride is high because:
options: Defective CFTR prevents chloride reabsorption in the duct
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: CFTR dysfunction prevents duct reabsorption of chloride, so sweat chloride is elevated (basis of the sweat test).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Botulinum toxin reduces sweating in hyperhidrosis by:
options: Blocking acetylcholine release at cholinergic nerve endings
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release at the cholinergic fibres supplying eccrine glands, reducing sweating.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a disease of which glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Hidradenitis suppurativa is chronic inflammation of apocrine-gland-bearing skin (axillae/groin).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Miliaria ('heat rash') is caused by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Miliaria results from obstruction of eccrine sweat ducts, trapping sweat and causing a vesicular rash.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which secretion mechanism do eccrine glands use?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands secrete by the merocrine mode (exocytosis) with no loss of cytoplasm.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The secretory coil differs from the duct histologically in that it is:
options: Larger and paler with myoepithelial cells
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: The secretory coil is larger, paler and has peripheral myoepithelial cells; the duct is smaller, darker and two-layered.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which gland type is the true thermoregulator?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands provide thermoregulatory sweating; apocrine glands are scent-related.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Compared with eccrine glands, apocrine glands are controlled by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands are sympathetic adrenergic; eccrine glands are sympathetic cholinergic.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Absent or reduced sweat glands causing heat intolerance is seen in:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Ectodermal dysplasia can feature reduced/absent sweat glands, causing anhidrosis and heat intolerance.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which statement correctly pairs a gland with its opening?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands open into the hair follicle, whereas eccrine glands open onto the skin surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The layers of the cornea from anterior to posterior are:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Anterior to posterior: epithelium → Bowman's layer → stroma → Descemet's membrane → endothelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Corneal transparency depends on:
options: Regular collagen arrangement in the stroma and the endothelial water pump
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Regular stromal collagen spacing plus the endothelial pump keep the cornea dehydrated and transparent.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The corneal endothelium is important because it:
options: Pumps water out of the stroma to keep the cornea clear
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The endothelium pumps water out of the stroma; it does not regenerate, so its loss causes corneal oedema.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The cornea receives its oxygen mainly from:
options: The tear film (atmospheric oxygen) and aqueous humour
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Being avascular, the cornea is oxygenated by the tear film and aqueous humour (and nourished at the limbus).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: In the retina, the correct signal pathway is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Light signals pass photoreceptor → bipolar cell → ganglion cell → optic nerve.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Which photoreceptors mediate colour and high-acuity vision, and where are they concentrated?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Cones mediate colour and acuity and are concentrated at the fovea; rods mediate dim/night vision peripherally.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) does all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Transmit action potentials to the brain
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The RPE supports photoreceptors (phagocytosis, vitamin A, barrier, light absorption) but does not conduct impulses.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The fovea is characterised by:
options: Cones only and the highest visual acuity
A rich capillary network over the photoreceptors
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The fovea contains only cones and gives the highest acuity; it is an avascular pit.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The blind spot of the eye corresponds to the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The optic disc, where axons exit and vessels enter, has no photoreceptors and forms the blind spot.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Rods contain which photopigment and mediate which vision?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Rods use rhodopsin (which requires vitamin A) for dim/night vision.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Lens fibres achieve transparency by:
options: Losing organelles and packing with crystallins
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Mature lens fibres lose their nuclei/organelles and are filled with regularly arranged crystallin proteins.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: During accommodation for near vision, the ciliary muscle contracts and:
options: Zonules tighten and the lens flattens
Zonules relax and the lens becomes more rounded
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Ciliary muscle contraction relaxes the zonules, letting the elastic lens round up to increase refractive power.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Aqueous humour is produced by the ______ and drains via the ______.
options: ciliary body; trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The ciliary body secretes aqueous, which drains through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Glaucoma is characterised by:
options: Raised intraocular pressure with optic-nerve damage and disc cupping
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Impaired aqueous drainage raises IOP, damaging the optic nerve and cupping the disc.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: A painless progressive opacification of the lens is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Cataract is opacification of the lens crystallins, causing painless progressive visual loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Drusen and RPE/photoreceptor damage at the macula characterise:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Age-related macular degeneration features drusen and RPE/photoreceptor damage, causing central vision loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Retinal detachment is separation of the:
options: Neural retina from the retinal pigment epithelium
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Retinal detachment is separation of the neural retina from the underlying RPE, causing field loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy affects which corneal layer, causing what?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Loss of corneal endothelial cells in Fuchs' dystrophy impairs the water pump, causing corneal oedema.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Retinitis pigmentosa is a progressive degeneration primarily of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Retinitis pigmentosa is progressive rod degeneration, causing night blindness and tunnel vision.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The histological hallmark of retinoblastoma is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Retinoblastoma shows Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes and is linked to RB1 gene mutation.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The organ of Corti is located on the:
options: Basilar membrane in the scala media
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The organ of Corti (the hearing sensory organ) sits on the basilar membrane within the scala media.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The main afferent (sensory) cells of hearing are the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Inner hair cells are the primary sensory cells; outer hair cells amplify basilar-membrane motion.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Sound transduction occurs when hair-cell stereocilia bend against the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Basilar-membrane vibration bends the stereocilia against the tectorial membrane, depolarising the hair cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The endolymph of the scala media is characteristically high in:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Endolymph is high in K+ (produced by the stria vascularis); perilymph is high in Na+.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Endolymph is secreted by the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The stria vascularis in the cochlear duct wall produces the K+-rich endolymph.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: According to cochlear tonotopy, high frequencies are detected at the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The stiff narrow base detects high frequencies; the wide floppy apex detects low frequencies.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Which cranial nerve carries auditory and vestibular signals?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) carries hearing (cochlear) and balance (vestibular) signals.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The maculae of the utricle and saccule detect:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Maculae detect linear acceleration and gravity via otolith-weighted hair cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The cristae ampullares of the semicircular canals detect:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Cristae ampullares detect angular acceleration via hair cells projecting into the cupula.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Otoliths (otoconia) are found in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Otoliths sit on the otolithic membrane of the maculae, weighting them to respond to gravity/linear acceleration.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The pinna is composed of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The pinna is elastic cartilage covered by skin.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Ceruminous glands of the ear canal are modified:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Ceruminous glands (earwax) are modified apocrine glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Which ossicle transmits vibration to the oval window?
